definition: Amalgamation means the process or result of blending separate, distinct things — traditions, substances, or organizations — into one new whole.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word amalgamation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know amalgamation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Modern English is an amalgamation of Anglo-Saxon, Norse, Norman French, and Latin, each conquest and contact folding new vocabulary into a single language.
Collection is the weakest: a collection is just distinct things gathered side by side with no blending at all, while an amalgamation makes them into one new whole.
Mixture is weaker: in a mixture the ingredients sit together but stay recognizably separate, while an amalgamation blends them into one new whole.
Fusion is stronger: an amalgamation still lets a careful eye trace the original parts, but a fusion melts them together so completely that no seams remain.

A blend is a smooth combining in which the parts soften into each other — a blended coffee, a blended tone. An amalgamation insists the sources were genuinely distinct — different traditions, companies, languages — before they were folded into one new whole. Similar things blend easily; an amalgamation unites true differents.

A composite is a whole assembled from parts that keep doing their separate jobs, like a composite photo or a composite material. An amalgamation goes further: its ingredients are blended into one new thing rather than fitted together, so the joints stop mattering.

A synthesis is the deliberate combining of ideas or findings into a new whole, and it lives mostly in the world of thought — a synthesis of two theories. An amalgamation can merge anything — firms, styles, languages — and stresses the blended result more than the reasoning.

Amalgam is a Medieval Latin word for a soft, blended mass — dentists still call a mixed-metal filling an amalgam. The two rival student newspapers voted to amalgamate: they joined into one combined weekly paper.
Amalgamation means the process or result of blending separate, distinct things — traditions, substances, or organizations — into one new whole.

Three formerly separate companies with distinct specialties have been combined into one new organization, and amalgamation names exactly that result of merging different parts into a single whole.

The city of Budapest did not exist before 1873.

On one bank of the Danube stood Buda, a hilly royal town of castles and thermal baths; across the river sprawled Pest, a flat, fast-growing commercial center; to the north sat quiet Óbuda with its Roman ruins.
The amalgamation of the three into a single capital was argued over for decades before parliament finally approved it.
Within a generation, the seams had faded: one government, one police force, and bridges that made the river feel less like a border than a main street.
Residents today call themselves neither Budans nor Pestians but simply citizens of the city the merger made.
